passages.text: INFLUENZA, an epidemic catarrhal fever, which at times spreads over whole countries, and even over the greater part of Europe, in a few weeks.
The name is Italian, and was given because the disease was ascribed to the influence of the stars.
It begins with chilliness, pain of the head and limbs, sneezing, a running from the eyes and nose, and a troublesome cough, with great weakness out of proportion to the fever.
Its cause is some peculiar state of the atmosphere, for it attacks whole cities at once, and could not spread so fast by contagion from one person to another.
Remarkable epidemics of this kind happened in 1762, 1775, and 1782.
It is seldom fatal, except to old persons and to those already weakened by disease of the lungs.
The cure is by rest, warm diluting drinks, and gentle sweating; bleeding is to be used with caution, as the weakness is great.

Influenza, commonly known as the flu, is an infectious disease caused by influenza viruses. Symptoms range from mild to severe and often include fever, runny nose, sore throat, muscle pain, headache, coughing and fatigue.
The word comes from the Italian influenza, meaning influence. Epidemics were once blamed on the influence of the stars; the word entered English in the 18th century.
The virus spreads from person to person through the air in droplets and small particles produced when infected people cough, sneeze or talk, and through contaminated surfaces.
Seasonal epidemics cause 290,000 to 650,000 deaths each year. People at highest risk include the elderly, young children, pregnant women and people with chronic illness.
The 1918 pandemic infected about a third of the world's population and killed tens of millions of people.
Human influenza virus was first isolated in 1933 by Wilson Smith, Christopher Andrewes and Patrick Laidlaw.
Yearly vaccination is the main way to prevent the disease. Most people recover with rest and fluids, and antiviral drugs such as oseltamivir can shorten the illness.

reasons: Both explain the Italian name and the influence of the stars.
Spanish flu scores well but covers only the 1918 pandemic, so it is a second candidate.

alignments.label: The name

britannica.quote: ascribed to the influence of the stars

wikipedia.quote: Epidemics were once blamed on the influence of the stars

alignments.note: Both tell the same story of the name. Neither treats the stars as the cause.

alignments.label: Symptoms

britannica.quote: pain of the head and limbs, sneezing, a running from the eyes and nose, and a troublesome cough

wikipedia.quote: runny nose, sore throat, muscle pain, headache, coughing

alignments.note: The same list in modern words.

alignments.label: Great weakness

britannica.quote: great weakness out of proportion to the fever

alignments.note: The 1823 entry notes the weakness more sharply than the modern summary.

alignments.label: The cause

britannica.quote: Its cause is some peculiar state of the atmosphere

alignments.note: A state of the air is replaced by a virus, isolated in 1933.

alignments.label: Not contagious

britannica.quote: could not spread so fast by contagion from one person to another

wikipedia.quote: The virus spreads from person to person through the air

alignments.note: The speed that seemed to rule out contagion is explained by airborne spread.

alignments.label: Who is at risk

britannica.quote: except to old persons and to those already weakened by disease of the lungs

wikipedia.quote: People at highest risk include the elderly

alignments.note: Same groups at risk. Wikipedia adds young children and pregnant women.

alignments.label: Rest and drinks

britannica.quote: The cure is by rest, warm diluting drinks

wikipedia.quote: Most people recover with rest and fluids

alignments.note: The advice has hardly changed. The 1823 caution about bleeding is no longer needed.

alignments.label: The 1918 pandemic

wikipedia.quote: The 1918 pandemic infected about a third of the world's population

alignments.note: The worst outbreak came almost a century after this edition.

wikipedia.quote: Yearly vaccination is the main way to prevent the disease

suggestedQuestions: Why did the 1823 entry think influenza was not contagious?
Where does the name influenza come from?
Has the advice for treating influenza changed since 1823?

Why did the 1823 entry think influenza w.answer: Because it attacked whole cities at once, and the entry judged that no contagion between people could spread so fast; it blamed a state of the atmosphere instead [B4]. Wikipedia says the virus spreads from person to person through the air in droplets and small particles [W3], which explains the speed.

Where does the name influenza come from?.answer: From Italian. Both texts say the disease was blamed on the influence of the stars [B2] [W2]. Wikipedia adds that the word entered English in the 18th century [W2].

Has the advice for treating influenza ch.answer: Less than for most diseases. In 1823 the cure was rest, warm drinks and gentle sweating, with caution about bleeding [B7]. Today most people recover with rest and fluids, antiviral drugs can shorten the illness, and yearly vaccination prevents it [W7].
